For example, Dahui taught people exclusively to look at the huatou and to lay on a ruthless hand (laying a ruthless hand on greed, anger, delusion, and idle thought), only wanting you to kill off the stealing mind (the mind that reaches out after conditions) entirely. As for example he said in addressing the assembly: “In investigating Chan you need only empty out the mind, and paste the two words ‘birth and death' on your forehead, as though you owed someone ten thousand strings of cash. Three hours by day and three by night, in tea and in rice, walking and standing, sitting and lying down, when exchanging courtesies with friends, in quiet and in noise — raise a huatou: ‘Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: No.' Just look at it this way and that. When it has no flavor, it is like butting against a wall; when you come to the knot, it is like a mouse entering a cow's horn, and then you will see the outcome (like a mouse entering a cow's horn, there is advance but no retreat, and you will see the end). I want you to prepare a long-enduring body and mind and wrestle with it (making long-term plans, resolving firmly, investigating with your whole body and mind, never apart from it for a moment, not resting until you awaken. The Gateless Gate of the Chan School says: “Take the three hundred and sixty joints and the eighty-four thousand pores, raise a mass of doubt through the whole body, and investigate the word ‘no,' raising it to mind day and night.”). Of a sudden the mind-flower blazes forth, illumining buddha-lands in the ten directions, and one awakening goes through to the bottom.” The passage above is the tongs and hammer that old man Dahui habitually used, and its meaning is simply that you should use the huatou to dam up the flow of idle thought beneath the mind-root so that it does not run on, and right at the place where it does not run on, look into and grasp your original face. It is not that you are taught to ponder over the kōan and take it as the mass of doubt, seeking an explanation. As for the words “the mind-flower blazes forth,” how could that be obtained from anywhere else (from the place of thought)?

[The stealing mind] What is called the stealing mind is the shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects, also called the consciousness of feeling, that is, the consciousness-mind. Chan Master Zhongfeng says: “What is the stealing mind? It is another name for the consciousness of feeling, because it can rob one of one's own supreme Dharma-wealth.” (The Extensive Record of Zhongfeng) [The six periods] In ancient India the day and night were divided into six periods: three by day and three by night. The three by day are morning, midday, and sunset; the three by night are early night, middle night, and late night. One such period equals four modern hours, so six periods make twenty-four hours. [To see the outcome] To clarify the causal relations or the outcome of a matter. [The flow of idle thought] The arising, ceasing, and shifting on of idle thought. [The flow of idle thought does not run on] The flow of idle thought comes to rest.

[As the Buddhas and patriarchs have one by one instructed above, they want you to investigate yourself, not to go seeking in mysterious and wonderful words and phrases. When people today investigate Chan and do the work, everyone speaks of looking at the huatou and bringing down the mass of doubt, but they do not know to investigate at the root; they only seek on the huatou. Seeking and seeking, of a sudden they think up a certain scene and say they are awakened; then they speak verses and present praises, treat it as rare merchandise, and think they have attained — never knowing that they have fallen entirely into the net of idle thought and views. In investigating Chan like this, do they not put out the eyes of people for generations to come?]

As the Buddhas and patriarchs have one by one instructed above, they want you to investigate yourself, not to go seeking in mysterious and wonderful words and phrases. When people today investigate Chan and do the work, everyone speaks of looking at the huatou and bringing down the mass of doubt, but they do not know to investigate at the root; they only seek on the huatou (pondering and guessing). Seeking and seeking, of a sudden they think up a certain scene and say they are awakened; then they speak verses and present praises, treat it as rare merchandise, and think they have attained — never knowing that they have fallen entirely into the net of idle thought and views. In investigating Chan like this, do they not put out the eyes of people for generations to come?

[Young people today have not yet sat steadily on the cushion before they claim to have awakened to the Way; they show off their tongues, play with the spirit-soul, take it for swift and sharp repartee, think up a few lines of groundless nonsense, and call it “praising the ancients.” All of it comes from your own idle thought — when did you ever dream of the ancients being present? If awakening to the Way were as easy for people today as this, then comparing them with the ancients' conduct — how Changqing sat until he wore out seven cushions, how Zhaozhou for thirty years did not let his mind stray — the ancients would be the dullest-rooted of people, not fit even to carry your straw sandals. People of overweening pride, claiming to have attained what they have not attained — should one not be afraid!]

Young people today have not yet sat steadily on the cushion before they claim to have awakened to the Way; they show off their tongues, play with the spirit-soul (the consciousness-spirit), take it for swift and sharp repartee, think up a few lines of groundless nonsense, and call it “praising the ancients.” All of it comes from your own idle thought — when did you ever dream of the ancients being present? If awakening to the Way were as easy for people today as this, then comparing them with the ancients' conduct — for example, Chan Master Hui Leng of Changqing in Fuzhou, who sat until he wore out seven cushions, and Chan Master Zhaozhou, who for thirty years did not let his mind stray — the ancients would be the dullest-rooted of people, not fit even to carry straw sandals for you people of today. These people of overweening pride, claiming to have attained what they have not attained — should one not be afraid!

[Conduct] Practice and bearing. [Claiming to have attained what one has not attained — should one not be afraid!] To claim to have attained what one has not attained is a great lying speech. In the noble path, to say one has attained when one has not, to say one has realized when one has not, and so to deceive the foolish and gain profit and offerings — all of this is called “great lying speech”; its offense is most heavy, and after death one falls into the great hells.

[In investigating Chan and looking at the huatou, bringing down the mass of doubt is absolutely indispensable. It is said: small doubt, small awakening; great doubt, great awakening; no doubt, no awakening. The point is only to use the doubt well: once the mass of doubt is broken, the Buddha's and patriarchs' nostrils are naturally strung through on one thread. Take the kōan of looking at reciting the Buddha's name: you only examine truly who it is that recites the Buddha's name, not doubt who the Buddha is. If you doubted who the Buddha is, then you need only hear a lecturer say that Amitābha Buddha is named Infinite Light, and you would thereby be awakened and produce a few verses on Infinite Light. If that were called awakening to the Way, then those who awaken to the mind would be as numerous as hemp and millet. How bitter! How bitter!]

In investigating Chan and looking at the huatou, bringing down the mass of doubt is absolutely indispensable. It is said: small doubt, small awakening; great doubt, great awakening; no doubt, no awakening. The point is only to use the doubt well: once the mass of doubt is broken, then you and the Buddha's and patriarchs' nostrils are naturally strung through on one thread. Take the kōan of looking at reciting the Buddha's name: you only examine truly “who it is that recites the Buddha's name,” not doubt who the Buddha is. If you doubted who the Buddha is, then you need only hear a lecturer say that Amitābha Buddha is named Infinite Light, and you would thereby be awakened and produce a few verses on Infinite Light. If that were called awakening to the Way, then those who awaken to the mind would be as numerous as hemp and millet. How bitter! How bitter!

[The ancients said: “A huatou is like a tile for knocking on the door; you only knock the door open to see the person inside, you do not do your business outside the door.” From this it is amply clear that when you raise doubt by means of the huatou, the doubt does not lie in the huatou — it must be at the root. Take the case of Jiashan studying under Chuanzi. Chuanzi asked: “A thousand feet of line let down, the intent is in the deep pool; three inches from the hook — why do you not speak?” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the master struck him with the oar and knocked him into the water. Jiashan had just climbed back into the boat when the master said again, “Speak! Speak!” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, the master struck him again. Jiashan was greatly awakened, and nodding three times, said: “The silk line at the pole's tip is yours to play with; not stirring the clear waves, the meaning is of itself apart.” If Jiashan had done his business on the hook and line, how could Chuanzi have given his life for him? This is how the ancients, quick and ready, were good at finding a way out.]

The ancients said: “A huatou is like a tile for knocking on the door; you only knock the door open to see the person inside (the intrinsic nature), you do not do your business outside the door.” From this it is amply clear that when you raise doubt by means of the huatou, the doubt does not lie in the huatou — it must be at the root. Take the case of Jiashan (Chan Master Shanhui) studying under Chuanzi (Chan Master Decheng). Chuanzi asked: “A thousand feet of line let down, the intent is in the deep pool; three inches from the hook — what do you say?” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, Chuanzi struck him with the oar and knocked him into the water. Jiashan had just climbed back into the boat when Chuanzi said again, “Speak! Speak!” As Jiashan was about to open his mouth, Chuanzi struck him again. Jiashan was greatly awakened, and nodding three times, said: “The silk line at the pole's tip is yours to play with; not stirring the clear waves, the meaning is of itself apart.” If Jiashan had done his business on the hook and line, how could Chuanzi have given his life for him? This is how the ancients, quick and ready, were good at finding a way out.

[Three inches from the hook] In his Dream-Wandering Collection, “Miscellaneous Words from Mount Jing,” Master Hanshan says: “Biting down on the huatou is not for the sake of understanding the huatou; you only borrow the huatou to raise doubt and cut off idle thought. Your investigation must be carried on at the place apart from the huatou; only when doubt is raised does it gain power. The ancient worthy said, ‘Three inches from the hook — why do you not speak?' Those before us have already marked it out (the ancients have already pointed it out). When the doubt reaches the point where feeling and consciousness do not arrive and words do not reach, and you are pressed to the utmost, a little glimmer of light bursts out — this is called the samādhi of lightning. This is just the time to advance; do not rejoice. If you take this as it, you will be satisfied with little, and your whole person will be covered over by this bit of light, unable to emerge again. When it comes out afterward, you will be entirely at its command.” [How could Chuanzi have given his life for him?] See in full the note on Chuanzi in “2. The Mind of Loyalty and Righteousness” above.

[In former times, when the Chan Way flourished, there were clear-eyed good teachers everywhere. Many pilgrim monks throughout the land investigated, and everywhere there was opening and awakening. Moreover it is said: it is not that there is no Chan, only that there are no teachers. Today the Chan community has been desolate for a long while. How fortunate that at this time many have aroused the resolve to investigate! Yet although there are good teachers, some measure the faculties and advance them provisionally, and confirm them according to sentiment. Students' minds are shallow, and they take it for attainment; and they do not believe the Tathāgata's noble teachings, do not seek the true road, but only do things muddledly, and so take the winter-melon seal as the final confirmation. Not only do they mislead themselves — they mislead others as well. Should one not be afraid!]

In former times, when the Chan Way flourished, there were clear-eyed good teachers everywhere. Many pilgrim monks throughout the land investigated, and everywhere there was awakening. Moreover it is said: it is not that there is no Chan, only that there are no teachers. Today the Chan community has been desolate for a long while. How fortunate that at this time many have aroused the resolve to investigate! Yet although there are good teachers, they instead measure the faculties and advance them provisionally, and confirm them according to sentiment (confirming by feeling and consciousness). Students' minds are shallow, and they take it for attainment; and they do not believe the Tathāgata's noble teachings, do not seek the true road, but only do things muddledly, and so take the winter-melon seal as the true confirmation (as the final decision). Not only do they mislead themselves — they mislead others as well. Should one not be afraid!

[Nazi] Also called the nazi monk: another name for a Chan monk, because Chan monks mostly wear a patchwork robe and wander in all directions. [Opening and awakening] Bringing the mind-ground to understanding, that is, awakening. [Winter-melon seal] A seal carved from winter-melon rind — a metaphor for a false and unreal confirmation. [Seal] A stamp used as a credential. [Final decision] The sense is to pass sentence; here it means a teacher's confirmation of a student's level of realization.

[Even among the officials and laymen of old, those recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp are only a few. Among the people of toil today, they do not keep even the coarse precepts, and their idle thoughts are turbid and confused. Relying on their own cleverness, they read a few occasions of the ancient worthies, and each one prides himself on being of the very highest faculties; on seeing a monk they at once contend in sharp repartee, and also take themselves to be awakened to the Way. Though this is the fault of the times, it is truly because we of the Sangha are one blind man leading a crowd of blind men. The old man now follows the true and essential points of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' work, and discusses them with you all; the wise and accomplished will of themselves have a way to set it right.]

Moreover, even among the officials and laymen of old, those recorded in the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp are only a few. Among the laypeople of today (people of toil), they do not keep even the coarse precepts, and their idle thoughts are turbid and confused. Relying on their own small cleverness, they read a few occasions of the ancient worthies, and so each one prides himself on being of the very highest faculties; on seeing a monk they at once contend in sharp repartee, and also think themselves truly awakened to the Way. Though this is the fault of the present age, it is also because we and others are one blind man leading a crowd of blind men. The old man now follows the true and essential points of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' work and discusses them with you all; the wise and accomplished will of themselves have a way to set it right.
